日本笙音色溫潤而空靈，具有獨特的古典韻味。其音質偏暗沉而內斂，帶有蒼涼感，卻不失: The Japanese shō has a warm, ethereal tone with a distinctive classical character. Its sound is on the dark, restrained side, with a bleak quality that is still elegant. The shō's range lies mainly in the upper middle register, and its tone is rich in layers, able to sound several pitches at once and so form harmony. The resonance of the wind chest and the bamboo pipes gives the sound a floating, three-dimensional quality, and its volume is gentle rather than harsh. Compared with Western wind instruments such as the bright, sharp oboe, the shō is gentler and more inward; compared with the flute it has more weight. Its unusual mechanism of sounding on both inhaling and exhaling lets the shō produce a distinctive echo and resonance, like layers of harmony stacked together, creating a quiet, solemn atmosphere in traditional gagaku.

笙（日本）以十七根長短不一的竹管構成，傳統選用薄壁天然竹材。竹管垂直插入杯狀木製: The Japanese shō is built from seventeen bamboo pipes of different lengths, traditionally of thin-walled natural bamboo. The pipes are set vertically into a cup-shaped wooden wind chest, usually made of light wood and coated with Japanese lacquer to keep it airtight and durable. Each sounding pipe has a free metal reed at its base, usually of a copper alloy and lacquered, fixed with a mixture of heated beeswax and pine resin. A silver or silver-plated mouthpiece is fitted at the side, and decorative metal rings hold the bamboo pipes. Tuning uses a lead-containing wax-resin mixture to alter the mass of the reeds.
笙（日本）是源自中國笙的日本自由簧氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs編號: The shō (Japan) is a Japanese free-reed aerophone derived from the Chinese sheng, Hornbostel–Sachs number 412.13. The instrument has 17 bamboo pipes of different lengths set vertically into a cup-shaped wooden wind chest, with metal free reeds at the base of the pipes; two of the pipes do not sound and are kept to preserve the symmetrical shape. It sounds whether the player breathes in or out, so it can be blown continuously. Traditionally it is one of the three main wind instruments of Japanese gagaku, accompanying the melody with aitake tone clusters, and it also appears in contemporary solo and ensemble music.
笙（日本）為氣鳴自由簧樂器，源自中國笙，於奈良時代（西元710至794年）傳入日: The shō (Japan) is a free-reed aerophone derived from the Chinese sheng; it reached Japan in the Nara period (710–794 AD) and is now used almost only in gagaku. In the Heian period the two silent pipes were occasionally still sounded along with the piece; the larger u, derived from the Chinese yu, fell out of use later and was revived at the end of the twentieth century by Hiromi Yoshida and Ko Ishikawa. From the middle of the twentieth century Japanese composers wrote solo and ensemble works for it; after John Cage met Mayumi Miyata at the Darmstadt Summer Courses in 1990 he wrote several Number Pieces for her. Later works by Stephan Micus, Björk and others carried it further internationally, and Koichi Wakata took it to the International Space Station.
